w: Pink-red walls dominate Prešeren Square -- the colour marks the Franciscan order. The church rose 1646-1660 on a site that already held two or three earlier ones; Matevž Langus painted the frescoes, Francesco Robba carved the Baroque altar in 1736. A monument of national significance since 2008.
s: Pink church on Prešeren Square, marking the Franciscan order
_facts: Built 1646-1660 on a site with two or three earlier churches; bell towers followed around 1720
Exterior redesigned in 1858; interior frescoes added mid-19th century by Matevž Langus and, on the ceiling, Matej Sternen
Main altar mostly the work of Baroque sculptor Francesco Robba, 1736
Red/pink colour symbolic of the Franciscan order; protected as a cultural monument of national significance since 2008

a: Center district, near Tivoli City Park
w: Slovenia's oldest scientific institution shares its building with the Museum of Natural History, near Tivoli Park. Downstairs, the numismatics department holds old coins and banknotes alongside archaeological finds and applied-arts displays -- honoured in 2021 with the golden Order for Exceptional Merits.
s: Slovenia's oldest museum, coins and antiquities together
_facts: Along with the Slovenian Museum of Natural History in the same building, it is the country's oldest scientific and cultural institution
Extensive archaeological artefact collection, plus a numismatics department of old coins and banknotes on the ground floor
Also displays related to the applied arts
Awarded the golden Order for Exceptional Merits by President Borut Pahor in 2021

w: Ljubljana's largest park sprawls from the Center district toward Šiška, Vič and Rožnik Hill, scattered with notable buildings and artworks along its paths. Protected since 1984 as part of the Tivoli-Rožnik Hill-Šiška Hill Nature Park, and home to a wide variety of birds.
_facts: Largest park in Ljubljana, stretching from the Center district toward Šiška, Vič and Rožnik districts
Several notable buildings and art works stand within it
Protected since 1984 as part of the Tivoli-Rožnik Hill-Šiška Hill Nature Park
Home to a variety of bird species

w: Seven former military barracks -- once Austro-Hungarian headquarters, later the Yugoslav People's Army's -- have stood squatted since September 1993, turned into an autonomous cultural centre. It takes its name from the street next door, itself named for a 19th-century priest and language reformer.
s: Squatted army barracks, an autonomous zone since 1993
_facts: Formerly the military headquarters of the Austro-Hungarian Army, then the Slovenian HQ of the Yugoslav People's Army
Seven buildings (military barracks) over 12,500 square metres, squatted since September 1993
Full name: Autonomous Cultural Centre Metelkova City (Avtonomni kulturni center Metelkova mesto)
Named after nearby Metelkova ulica, itself named for 19th-century priest and language reformer Fran Metelko

a: Rudnik district, along the Gruber Canal
w: The oldest botanical garden in Southeastern Europe opened under Franc Hladnik in 1810. Over 4,500 plant species and subspecies now pack two hectares along the Gruber Canal, roughly a third native to Slovenia, traded with more than 270 gardens worldwide.
s: Southeastern Europe's oldest botanical garden, since 1810
_facts: Oldest botanical garden in Southeastern Europe, operating since 1810 under founder Franc Hladnik
Over 4,500 plant species and subspecies on 2 hectares, roughly a third endemic to Slovenia
Member of Botanic Gardens Conservation International, cooperating with more than 270 botanical gardens worldwide
Located in the Rudnik district along the Gruber Canal

w: Ljubljana's oldest stadium has sat closed since 2008, silent since architect Jože Plečnik built it from 1925 for a Catholic youth sports association. It later became the football home of NK Olimpija Ljubljana until the club folded in 2005.
s: Plečnik's oldest stadium in the city, closed since 2008
_facts: Oldest stadium in Ljubljana, construction begun 1925 for the Catholic youth sport association Orel
Designed by architect Jože Plečnik
Closed since 2008
Home of NK Olimpija Ljubljana until the club's dissolution in 2005, then NK Bežigrad between 2005 and 2007

w: The seat of Slovenia's national opera and ballet company sits at Župančičeva 1, boxed in by heavyweight neighbours -- the Slovenian Parliament on one side, the National Museum and National Gallery on the other. Home to the Ljubljana Slovene National Theatre Opera and Ballet.
s: Opera house wedged between Parliament and the museums
_facts: Seat of the national opera and ballet company, the Ljubljana Slovene National Theatre Opera and Ballet
Serves as the national opera building of Slovenia
Stands at 1 Župančičeva Street, between the Slovenian Parliament and the National Museum/National Gallery

a: Trnovo, in front of Trnovo Church
w: A bridge has crossed the Gradaščica here since the late 17th century, linking Krakovo and Trnovo, Ljubljana's oldest suburbs. The current wide, tree-lined version went up 1928-1932 to Jože Plečnik's design -- UNESCO-listed as part of his legacy since 2021.
_facts: A bridge has stood on the site since the late 17th century, crossing the Gradaščica River
Connects Krakovo and Trnovo, the oldest Ljubljana suburbs, known for market gardens
Current bridge built 1928-1932 by constructor Matko Curk to plans by architect Jože Plečnik
Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List since August 2021 as part of Plečnik's legacy

w: Decades of effort by the Islamic Community of Slovenia finally landed a home in the Bežigrad district: officially the Islamic Religio-Cultural Center, known simply as the Ljubljana mosque. The complex holds a library, a classroom, an ablution fountain and the Imam's quarters.
s: Decades in the making, Ljubljana's mosque and cultural centre
_facts: Officially the Islamic Religio-Cultural Center, in the Bežigrad district
The culmination of a decades-long effort by the Islamic Community of Slovenia
Complex includes a library, a classroom, an ablution fountain and the Imam's offices and quarters

a: encircling the city, past Koseze Pond and Golovec Hill
w: Thirty-three kilometres of gravel path trace the line where Fascist Italy strung barbed wire around Ljubljana in 1942, sealing it off from the Partisans in the hills beyond. The wire came down in 1945; the memorial trail, built 1974-1985, carries 102 stones marking old bunker positions.
s: The wartime barbed-wire line, now a 33km memorial trail
_facts: Nearly 33km gravel walkway around Ljubljana, following the route of a WWII Italian barbed-wire fence (Feb 1942 to June 1945)
Built to cut off the city's Liberation Front activists from Slovene Partisans in the countryside
Trail construction started 1974, completed 1985
Marked by 102 octagonal memorial stones (designer Vlasto Kopač) at former bunker positions, and 7,400 trees of 49 species
